I lost my dad a few years ago to lung cancer, and it's tough. The worst part of it all is watching the person you knew your whole life dissolve into someone mentally unknown and physically frail. It sucks, and there's no real way around it. Two things helped me get though it: alone time to reflect on things for myself, and a caring friend to just share some beers with. Sometimes you just need that time alone or with a friend to just absorb what is happening and emotionally decompress. Be there for your family, but make sure you take time for yourself.
Remember that people only truly die when their memory fades. Remember him and honor his memory and you and your family will do fine :D

Prepare yourself, spend quality time with your father if you can. Take him out for a snort of whiskey, ballgame, museum, car show or whatever you know he would enjoy. Not saying smother him all the time, but get some time in and get that last one fishing trip in. Next is to spend time helping out with his care. This is the most unpleasant part, but once his time comes knowing how low the quality of life was for him and caregivers give a sense of relief that helps with the loss.

You can't stop what's going to happen. We all die. You, your wife, any children that you may have, will die. It is life. More importantly, it's okay. It's okay to die. No one has ever told us that, but death is okay. It happens to us all. I take heart in knowing that the ones I've lost would never want me to be troubled over it. I'm certain that they would want me to continue, to be the best that I can, to console the ones around me, to prosper, to live. When I die, that would be all I want.

There is no dealing with it. It is what it is. We just have to move on. We don't have to forget them or silence their memory or turn away from all the experiences we had with them, but we do have to continue on with life. In my experience, the hurt never goes away, but the memories persist and inspire me. I ascribe to the idea that no one is dead until they've been forgotten. What people have left this world before me, I remember. I will always remember. They are not dead. They are very much alive in my thoughts. Past the grave, they continue to encourage me. Their wisdom persists. They teach me as many things dead as they did alive. Aaaand, that's all I've got.

First of all, I'm so sorry you are going through this. Both of my parents have died, and it sucks.

Everyone else here has already given you good pointers, so instead of repeating their advice, I just wanted to add:

Everyone grieves in a different way. Some people want others close by, some need time alone to process. For some, it's done in a couple of months. Other take years. It will be easier if you stay true to yourself, and give the other people who are hurting the space they need to do the same.

Depending on your friends, some of them might have a hard time being around you. Because they won't know what to say or do, because they have issues themselves or because your dad's mortality impresses on them the fact that their parents (and they themselves) are mortal, too. If you need help, ask them, because otherwise they might not act due to not knowing the right course of action to take. But do lean on them, that's what friends are for during times like this.

If you find yourself mourning to the point where functioning gets difficult (eating, sleeping, etc), either go to your physician or ask your wife to 'force' you to take care of yourself. Be careful with sleep medication - it is addictive as fuck.

Also, be prepared for there to be a hole, a void, in your life. For a while, the hole will be the most important thing. It will take up your energy, time and attention. It's big and there to stay. Then you will notice that there's still life beyond the hole, and that will be unfair, and painful. At a certain point, though, your attention will shift away from the hole. That's okay. Don't feel guilty. You're still alive, and you're allowed to live. Then there will be times when that hole is suddenly back in full view in front of you, and it'll grab you by the throat and hurt, hurt, hurt. But that will happen less and less, and as you live on, the pain will both be more poignant (your dad won't be there for big events in your life) and farther removed from you, as that person isn't on your journey any longer (as with a former best friend you haven't seen in 10 years. If you meet them again, you'll still love them, but it's less profound, because they don't know the current you and you don't know the current them).

Make sure you spend some time thinking of the positive things, the happy memories. You don't want your foremost thought about your father to be about his death. He had a bigger impact on your life than that.

I wish you strength, peace of mind and time to heal.

ps: Don't forget to tell your dad the things you still want to tell him. It helps.
